chunks: What a via is and why. The question: What is a via? Why are they needed?
A via is a small plated hole through a circuit board that connects copper on one layer to copper on another.
A board has several layers, and a trace can only run flat along one of them. A via lets a signal, power or heat move up or down between layers. It is not a perfect wire, though.
It has a little resistance (opposition to steady current), inductance and capacitance (it stores a little charge).
Think of an elevator in an office building. Each floor is a layer, and the hallways are traces. To get from one floor to another you need the elevator shaft, which is the via.
The shaft runs through every floor, even if you only stop at two, so it takes space on all of them. And the elevator is not instant: at high speeds it holds up traffic.
A through via on a 4-layer board. The barrel is a thin tube, so the middle is hollow.
It lands on pads on L1 and L4, while the plane layers have a void (antipad) so the barrel doesn't short to them.
Layer: one flat sheet of copper in the board's stack. Boards often have four or more. Trace: a copper line that carries a signal along one layer.
Barrel: the copper-plated wall of the hole, like a thin copper tube. Pad: a copper ring on a layer that the barrel connects to.
Inductance: how strongly a wire resists fast changes in current. 1 nanohenries is a billionth of a henry.
Take a common via: a 0. 3 mm hole through a 1. 6 mm board. Its resistance is only about 1. 3 milliohms, so 1 amps through it loses about 1. 3 millivolts.
Its inductance is about 1. 3 nanohenries. At slow speeds you can ignore it. At 1 gigahertz the same 1. 3 nanohenries acts like about 8 ohms, which is large.
That is why fast designs count their vias and put a ground via next to each signal via.
That is the whole idea: a via connects layers, but it is a small circuit element, not a free wire.
"A via is a plated hole that electrically connects copper on different layers of a PCB.
We need them because traces only run in 2-D on each layer, so signals have to drop through the stack to cross each other, reach power and ground planes, escape from BGAs, and move heat.
A via isn't ideal: a typical one is about a milliohm, around 1 nanohenries and a few tenths of a picofarad, so at high frequency I treat it as a small inductor and keep return paths close."
